title: How Visa Really Makes Money
the_thought: Visa gets paid to carry the yes.
hook: You tap a Visa card on a little black slab. The slab beeps. You walk out with a cup. But Visa did not lend you a dollar. Why does a company that never issued the card, never roasted the beans, and never owned the shop still get paid for that tap? The coffee is not the product. The yes is.

levels.name: The Tap
beats: Most people think they know this company because they see the name every week. It sits on the plastic. It sits on the door sticker. It sits on the phone wallet. It looks like the company that is lending you money when dinner is over. That is the obvious business. A shopper. A seller. A card. A number that says you can pay later, or pay from a checking account, or pay from a prepaid pot. The brand is so ordinary that it disappears. Watch the counter, not the logo. The clerk does not call Visa to ask if you are good for four dollars. The clerk does not open a Visa vault. The clerk does not check a Visa loan file with your name on it. The clerk just needs a yes, fast enough that the line does not die. If Visa were the lender, the story would be simple. Interest. Late fees. A credit limit. A collections desk. But that is a bank story, so why is the payment network wearing the bank's costume? Visa's own annual report for fiscal 2025 says the opposite in plain language. Visa is not a financial institution. It does not issue cards. It does not extend credit. It does not set the rates and fees on the account in your pocket. It does not take the credit risk if you vanish. So the plastic is a costume. The costume works because millions of people already trust it. The costume is not the engine. Here is the first loop. If the company on the card is not lending, not issuing, and not selling the coffee, why is the name on the card at all? What did you actually use when you tapped? You used a road. You used a rulebook. You used a yes that had to jump through four desks before the clerk's slab could beep. That road is easy to miss because it is supposed to be invisible. A good payments network feels like nothing happened. That is the puzzle. Visa can sit in a transaction you make every day and still not be the company you think you paid.

levels.name: Four Desks
beats: A typical Visa purchase is not two people. It is four. Visa's 10-K calls this the four-party model, then admits the real world now also includes wallets, fintechs, and governments. The spine is still four desks. Desk one is you. You have a credential. A card, a phone, a number in an app. In fiscal 2025 Visa counted 4.9 billion of those credentials. Desk two is the seller. More than 175 million merchant locations, the company said for that same year. The seller wants money, not a story about networks. Desk three is the acquirer. That is usually a bank or a processor hired by the shop. The acquirer is the seller's doorway into the rails. Desk four is the issuer. That is the bank or credit union that actually gave you the credential. If it is credit, that issuer is the one taking the risk. If it is debit, that issuer is watching your balance. Visa sits between the last two desks. The shopper never sends Visa a monthly payment. The shop sends the sale to the acquirer. The acquirer sends a request through VisaNet. Visa sends that request to the issuer. The issuer says yes or no. The yes comes back down the same pipe. Later, clearing and settlement move the actual money between the banks. That hop can take less than a second. It is not a loan approval from Visa. It is a message. Authorization is the yes or no. Clearing is the cleanup of what actually happened. Settlement is the banks paying each other. Three ugly words that mean: can this go through, what exactly went through, and who owes whom at the end of the day. The shopper only hears the beep. The banks hear a ledger. If you want a picture, do not picture a vault. Picture a bright little pulse leaving the tap, hitting the acquirer, hitting the network, hitting the issuer, and racing home with a yes. The pulse is the product. So what does the shop think it paid for, and what did it actually buy? Visa can also process pieces of transactions that are not even Visa-branded, as a gateway. And some Visa-branded sales, depending on the rules of the country, may not run on Visa's network at all. The 10-K is blunt about that. If the processor uses the network, Visa may earn service fees and data processing fees. If the processor does not, Visa may earn only the service fee. The brand on the plastic and the pipe under the plastic are not the same thing. That is why a tap can look like one company and legally be a crowd.

levels.name: The Fat Line
beats: Now look at the merchant's statement, not the shopper's app. On many sales, the seller does not receive the full sticker price. A slice disappears. People call that slice "the Visa fee" because the logo was on the card. A lot of that slice is not Visa's. Visa's filing walks through the money. After a sale is authorized, the issuer posts it to the shopper's account. The issuer pays the acquirer an amount equal to the sale, minus an interchange reimbursement fee. The acquirer pays the seller the purchase amount minus a merchant discount rate. Interchange, in that telling, generally moves from the acquirer to the issuer. It is a balancing weight. It helps pay for rewards, fraud, and the cost of issuing plastic. Visa sets default interchange rates when nobody has negotiated something else. That is a strange power. It is also not the same thing as Visa putting interchange in its own till. The 10-K says the fees Visa receives from issuers and acquirers are not derived from interchange reimbursement fees or merchant discount rates. The acquiring bank, not Visa, usually sets what the shop is charged. Visa sets its own client fees on a separate track. But if the fat line is not Visa's profit, why does every argument about cards still land on Visa's desk? So the fat line on the receipt, the one that makes a cafe owner furious, is often a bank-to-bank transfer that Visa referees. The referee still gets paid. The referee is not taking home the whole argument. This is the first real surprise, and it opens a ruder question. If the big ugly number is mostly not Visa's, what is Visa's number? And why would a public company spend so much energy writing a fee table for money it does not collect? Because the table is how the four desks stay in the room. If interchange is too low, issuers get bored and push other plastic. If it is too high, sellers try to steer you to cash, to a rival network, or to a government rail. Visa's job is to keep the road crowded. The default rates are a steering wheel. They are not the fuel gauge.

levels.name: The Thin Pipe
beats: Visa's own till is a stack of client fees, then a huge rebate. In fiscal 2025, service revenue was 17.539 billion dollars. That line is for helping clients use the network and some issuing tools. Service revenue is recognized on payments volume from the prior quarter, which is a small accounting oddity with a big meaning. Visa gets paid for the last batch of spending, not for a guess about next month. Data processing revenue was 19.993 billion dollars. That is the pulse. Authorization, clearing, settlement, network access, fraud tools, acceptance tools. It is the closest thing Visa has to a meter on the pipe. International transaction revenue was 14.166 billion dollars. Cross-border sales and currency conversion. A tourist tap, an online order that hops a border, a currency switch. This line is why a network that looks domestic in your wallet can get much richer when money leaves the country. Other revenue was 4.053 billion dollars. Advisory work, some issuing services, brand and technology licenses, extras. It is the growing attic, not the foundation. Add those four lines and you get a fat gross pile. Then Visa hands a shocking amount back. Client incentives in fiscal 2025 were 15.751 billion dollars. They are recorded as a reduction of revenue. The annual report is clear about why they exist. Visa pays financial institutions, sellers, and other partners to grow volume, grow acceptance, and keep the brand on the plastic. That is the strange decision that makes the model make sense. Visa does not win by squeezing every possible penny out of a bank on day one. Visa wins by making Visa the default rail inside that bank's product meeting. Incentives are not a side charity. They are how a network buys the next billion credentials. After incentives, net revenue was 40.0 billion dollars. That is the number the company puts on the flag. It is also the number you have to read as "after paying the people who issue and accept the cards." So the fee looks small, but the rebate is huge. Why pay your own clients that much unless the loop dies without them? So the thin pipe has two truths at once. The processing and cross-border fees can be very valuable. And a large share of the headline is spent keeping the four desks loyal.

levels.name: Why Banks Stay
beats: Why does a bank keep paying for a road it does not own? Because a card with no doors is a toy. In fiscal 2025 Visa said it had nearly 14,500 financial institution clients and acceptance at more than 175 million merchant locations. The shopper does not choose a network in a vacuum. The shopper chooses a wallet that works at the place they already stand. That is a loop, and it is not mystical. More credentials make more sellers want the mark on the door. More doors make more banks want the mark on the plastic. Each side is the reason the other side stays. Switching costs are not a contract clause you can see. They are the fear of being the weird card that fails at the pharmacy. Visa also sells fear in a useful way. Fraud tools. Tokenization. Rules that say who eats a bad charge. A bank can try to rebuild that stack. A bank cannot rebuild 4.9 billion credentials and 175 million doors over a weekend. The shopper stays for a dumber reason, and it still matters. Habit. The same tap. The same beep. Rewards that the issuer, not Visa, usually funds with interchange. Visa benefits from that habit without paying you a mile. But habit is not a contract. What happens if a new rail makes the habit unnecessary? There is a second loop for the seller. Accepting the mark is expensive. Refusing it can be more expensive. If enough customers only carry one rail, the seller's "no" is a speech, not a strategy. This is why copycats do not just print a prettier logo. A new network can have better software and still starve. It needs both sides at once. That is the moat people mean when they say network effect, and it is also why Visa keeps writing that interchange table. The table is one of the tools that keeps issuers from wandering. Notice who the real customer is in that sentence. You tap. The bank pays. Visa's 10-K is written to financial institution clients, not to the person holding the cup. That is why a product that feels free to a shopper can still be a tollbooth. The toll is collected one desk over. The next question is colder. If the loop is that strong, where does the money get large enough to look like a 40 billion dollar company? And what could still break it?

levels.name: The Tiny Cut
beats: Do not narrate a spreadsheet. Hold one comparison. In fiscal 2025, Visa's payments volume was 14.2 trillion dollars. Total volume, including cash access and related items, was 16.7 trillion. Processed transactions on Visa's networks were 257.5 billion. Net revenue was 40.0 billion. If you divide that net revenue by payments volume, you get about 28 cents of Visa net revenue for every 100 dollars of payments volume. That is not the fee on your coffee. Filings do not publish Visa's take on a typical 100 dollar U.S. sale, and inventing one would be a lie. It is a blended average across countries, products, and routes. Some hops are richer. Some Visa-branded sales barely touch the pipe. Still, the comparison does a job. The shop thinks in percents. The network can get rich on fractions of a percent if the volume is planetary. 28 cents next to 100 dollars looks small. 28 cents next to 14.2 trillion looks like a factory. So why does a thin fee throw off software-like profit? Because someone else owns the expensive parts. Operating income in fiscal 2025 was 23.994 billion dollars. That is about 60 cents of operating income for every dollar of net revenue. Software businesses dream about that shape. Visa gets it because the expensive part of a payment is often someone else's balance sheet. The issuer owns the loan. The shop owns the inventory. Visa owns the message. Cross-border is the loud room in that factory. International transaction revenue of 14.166 billion dollars sat next to 19.993 billion of data processing. A tourist tap can be worth more to the network than a grocery tap down the street. That is not a moral. It is a map. The more commerce hops a border, the more the pipe can charge for translation. The year did not stop in September 2025. In the fiscal third quarter of 2026, ended June 30, 2026, Visa reported 11.633 billion dollars of net revenue, up 14 percent from the same quarter a year earlier. Service revenue in that quarter was 4.922 billion dollars. Data processing rose to 6.0 billion. International transaction revenue was 3.9 billion. Other revenue was 1.496 billion. Client incentives were 4.7 billion. It processed 71.7 billion transactions in that quarter, up 10 percent. The machine was still taking taps. The mix can change. The four desks do not. If you want a $100 picture, here is the honest one. On many real sales, the seller loses a much fatter slice than 28 cents, and most of that slice is not Visa's. Visa's published economics are the thin remainder after incentives, averaged across a planet of volume. The mystery was never that the remainder is huge on one coffee. The mystery is that the remainder exists on so many coffees that it becomes a 40 billion dollar business.

levels.name: The Paper Stack
beats: A loop this large collects enemies. In fiscal 2025, GAAP net income grew only 2 percent even while net revenue grew 11 percent. The earnings release is not shy about why. Results included a 2.5 billion dollar litigation provision tied to the interchange multidistrict litigation and other legal matters, plus smaller charges for severance and leases. The fat line Visa does not collect still follows Visa home. Merchants sue over interchange. Governments cap it. The referee gets blamed for the foul. The 10-K reads like a world tour of price controls. The United States already caps certain debit interchange under the Dodd-Frank Act and limits network exclusivity, which is a polite way of saying some debit taps can be steered off Visa's pipe. In Europe, the Interchange Fee Regulation places an effective cap on consumer credit and consumer debit interchange for domestic and cross-border transactions inside the European Economic Area of 30 basis points and 20 basis points. That is a government thumb on the fat line. It does not have to mention Visa's processing fee to change Visa's life, because issuers who earn less interchange start asking Visa for cheaper access. Australia, New Zealand, and a list of other countries push rates down or talk about doing it. When default interchange cannot sit where issuers like it, Visa says the network can look less attractive, and clients ask for more incentives. That hits net revenue directly. Routing is the quiet threat inside those rules. If a processor can complete a Visa-branded sale without VisaNet, the data processing meter stops. The brand can still be on the plastic. The pulse can go missing. That is not a fan theory. It is in the company's own description of when it earns service revenue only. Then there are the new roads. Account-to-account rails. Instant bank payments. Wallets that want to skip cards. Experiments with tokens and stablecoins that want to move value without a four-desk hop. Visa is trying to sit on those roads too. Trying is not the same as owning them. None of this requires a fake collapse. The weakness is structural. Visa's profit depends on remaining the default messenger. Regulation, litigation, and new pipes all attack the default, not the logo. So the next minute is not a victory lap. It is the part of the story the merchant lawsuit already told: the fat line can wound the referee. So if the model is that powerful, what could break it? A world where the yes no longer needs Visa's pulse. Or a world where the yes still happens and governments decide the pulse may not be paid like software.

levels.name: Carry The Yes
beats: Put the pieces back on the counter. You tapped. Four desks woke up. A pulse ran. An issuer, not Visa, took the credit risk or checked the balance. An acquirer, not Visa, usually set the shop's discount. Interchange, if it moved, generally moved toward the issuer. Visa billed its clients for the road, paid a fortune in incentives to keep the road crowded, and in fiscal 2025 kept 40.0 billion dollars of net revenue on 14.2 trillion of payments volume. That is the real business. Visa gets paid to carry the yes. Not to lend the money. Not to own the shop. Not to print the rewards catalog. To be the company that can take a tap at a counter and return a decision before the clerk looks bored. The clever part is that the costume and the engine need each other. Without the name on the plastic, the four desks have nothing to agree on. Without the pulse, the name is a sticker. But people argue about the fat fee because they can see it. The thin pipe is quieter, and that is why it can look like a mystery even if you have used it since breakfast. Visa gets paid to carry the yes. Once you hear that sentence, the card in your wallet looks less like a loan and more like a ticket onto a road you never see. Mastercard built a very different public story on a rhyming set of desks. The colors change. The hop does not. If you want the rest of the machine, the long version is here. The short version is the tap you already did.
Mastercard built a very different public story on a rhyming set of desks. The colors change. The hop does not.
